name: finance_v1_dev
purpose: Financial-query test set (user goal 2026-10-19): crises/macro, views, figures, personal-scope refusals, whole-collection questions. Curated from chunks_v3_paragraph without running any retriever or model. Not yet split into dev/test. DEV half: used for search tuning.

cases.query: In the early-to-mid 1980s, when Volcker was bringing inflation down, did Buffett think the inflation threat was over, and what did that mean for his view of long-term bonds?

gold_claims.claim: He applauded Fed Chairman Volcker and the more moderate price increases, but his long-term inflation views stayed as negative as ever: like virginity, a stable price level can be maintained but not restored.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1981 letter (1981_p0026); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: In 1984 he said bonds are only as sound as a dollar, that the long-term outlook for dollars is dismal, that substantial inflation lies ahead, and that runaway inflation has a small but real chance.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1984 letter (1984_p0107); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: Even in 1984, with inflation sharply down, he said the huge-deficit fiscal policy made high inflation delayed (perhaps for a long time) but not avoided, with the potential for a runaway upward spiral.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1984 letter (1984_p0108); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: Because runaway inflation would hurt existing bonds even more than stocks, an all-bond portfolio carries a small but unacceptable 'wipe out' risk, so any long-bond purchase must clear a special hurdle.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1984 letter (1984_p0109); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: In 1986 he still shunned long-term bonds except in very special situations, because he feared much higher rates of inflation within the next decade.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1986 letter (1986_p0080); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: Already in 1979 he refused to lock in a price for money decades ahead, following Polonius: 'Neither a short-term borrower nor a long-term lender be.'
gold_claims.verification_note: 1979 letter (1979_p0056); unit=qualitative statement

cases.verification_note: 1979_p0056, 1981_p0026, 1984_p0107, 1984_p0108, 1984_p0109, 1986_p0080 supply the 6 claims (Like virginity; as sound as a dollar; not be avoided; wipe out; much higher rates of inflation; long-term lender). 1983_p0069 ('as pessimistic as ever' on inflation) is relevant context.

cases.query: How did Buffett think interest rates affect what stocks are worth, from the high-rate early 1980s to the low-rate years around 2020?

gold_claims.claim: With long-term taxable bonds yielding over 16% in 1981 while American business earned about 14% on equity, a typical American business was no longer worth one hundred cents on the dollar to individual owners.
required_terms: one hundred cents on the dollar
gold_claims.verification_note: 1981 letter (1981_p0032, 1981_p0033); unit=qualitative statement with figures

gold_claims.claim: In the 1997 letter he recalled that at the annual meeting earlier that year, with the Dow at 7,071 and long-term Treasury yields at 6.89%, he and Munger had said the market was not overvalued as long as rates held or fell and companies kept earning high returns on equity; rates had since fallen.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1997 letter (1997_p0088); unit=figure. The letter is dated February 27, 1998 (1997_p0123) and says 'At the annual meeting last year', i.e. the May 1997 meeting (announced for Monday, May 5 in 1996_p0118).

gold_claims.claim: Lower interest rates make every dollar of earnings more valuable, but late-1990s prices had eroded Graham's margin of safety.
required_terms: every dollar of earnings becomes more valuable
gold_claims.verification_note: 1997 letter (1997_p0089); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: He never forecasts rates, but in 2019 said that if rates near then-current levels lasted, equities would almost certainly do far better over time than long-term fixed-rate debt.
required_terms: Forecasting interest rates has never been our game
gold_claims.verification_note: 2019 letter (2019_p0055); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: In 2021 he found little to buy because low long-term interest rates push up the prices of all productive investments, whether stocks, apartments, farms or oil wells.
required_terms: push the prices of all productive investments upward
gold_claims.verification_note: 2021 letter (2021_p0043); unit=qualitative statement

cases.verification_note: 1981_p0032, 1981_p0033, 1997_p0088, 1997_p0089, 2019_p0055, 2021_p0043 supply the 5 claims (exceeded 16%; 6.89%; every dollar of earnings becomes more valuable; fixed-rate debt instruments; push the prices of all productive investments upward).

cases.query: What did Buffett say about the October 1987 stock market crash and what caused it?

gold_claims.claim: The Dow ended 1987 up only 2.3% after a roller-coaster year: Mr. Market was on a manic rampage until October and then suffered a sudden, massive seizure.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1987 letter (1987_p0092); unit=qualitative statement with figure

gold_claims.claim: He blamed professional money managers who treat stocks as tokens in a game, above all 'portfolio insurance', a stop-loss strategy that had $60 billion to $90 billion of equities on a hair trigger in mid-October 1987.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1987 letter (1987_p0093, 1987_p0094); unit=qualitative statement with figure

gold_claims.claim: It is dead wrong to conclude that small investors have no chance: volatility caused by irrational big money is ideal for true investors, who are hurt only if forced to sell at untoward times.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1987 letter (1987_p0097); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: During the October break a few stocks fell to prices that interested Berkshire, but it could not make meaningful purchases before they rebounded.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1987 letter (1987_p0098); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: In 1996 he recalled the destructive effects of portfolio insurance in the 1987 market crash, quoting a wag who said it was the computers that should have been jumping out of windows.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1996 letter (1996_p0043); unit=qualitative statement

cases.verification_note: 1987_p0092, 1987_p0093, 1987_p0094, 1987_p0097, 1987_p0098, 1996_p0043 supply the 5 claims (massive seizure; portfolio insurance; dead wrong; break in October; jumping out of windows).

cases.query: What did Buffett say about the 1998 collapse of Long-Term Capital Management and what it showed about risk in the financial system?

gold_claims.claim: In 1998 the leveraged, derivatives-heavy trading of a single hedge fund, Long-Term Capital Management, alarmed the Federal Reserve so much that it hastily orchestrated a rescue.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2002 letter (2002_p0082); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: Fed officials later testified that LTCM, a firm unknown to the public with only a few hundred employees, could have seriously threatened the stability of American markets.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2002 letter (2002_p0082, 2002_p0083); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: The affair paralyzed many parts of the fixed-income market for weeks, and it was still far from a worst-case scenario.
required_terms: paralyzed many parts of the fixed-income market
gold_claims.verification_note: 2002 letter (2002_p0083); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: LTCM used total-return swaps, which allow 100% leverage and make a joke of margin requirements.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2002 letter (2002_p0083, 2002_p0084); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: He saw a dangerous macro picture: credit risk concentrated in a few derivatives dealers who trade heavily with each other, so that linkage could let the troubles of one quickly infect the others.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2002 letter (2002_p0081); unit=qualitative statement

cases.verification_note: 2002_p0081, 2002_p0082, 2002_p0083, 2002_p0084 supply the 5 claims (Long-Term Capital Management; stability of American markets; far from a worst-case scenario; total-return swaps; Linkage). LTCM is discussed only in the 2002 letter.

cases.query: Give me Buffett's insights related to the 2008 crisis.

gold_claims.claim: As problems at major financial institutions came out in 2008, the credit market became non-functional, and by the fourth quarter the credit crisis plus falling home and stock prices had produced a paralyzing fear and a freefall in business activity.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2008 letter (2008_p0011); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: The Treasury and the Fed went 'all in'; such once-unthinkable doses would likely bring unwelcome aftereffects such as an onslaught of inflation, but strong, immediate government action was essential to avoid a total breakdown of the financial system.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2008 letter (2008_p0012, 2008_p0013); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: He was certain the economy would be in shambles throughout 2009 and beyond, but said that did not tell him whether the stock market would rise or fall.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2008 letter (2008_p0016); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: The market disarray helped Berkshire's buying: 'pessimism is your friend, euphoria the enemy', and it made three large investments on terms unavailable in normal markets.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2008 letter (2008_p0022); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: When the financial system went into cardiac arrest in September 2008, Berkshire was a supplier of liquidity rather than a supplicant, putting $15.5 billion into the business world at the peak of the crisis.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2009 letter (2009_p0021); unit=qualitative statement with figure

cases.verification_note: User example question. 2008_p0011, 2008_p0012, 2008_p0013, 2008_p0016, 2008_p0022 (2008 letter) and 2009_p0021 (2009 letter) supply the 5 claims (paralyzing fear; onslaught of inflation; in shambles throughout 2009; pessimism is your friend; supplier of liquidity).

cases.query: According to Buffett, what caused the housing and mortgage bust behind the 2008 crisis?

gold_claims.claim: He traced the bust to the 1997-2000 manufactured-housing fiasco (borrowers who shouldn't have borrowed financed by lenders who shouldn't have lent, down payments ignored, loans securitized and sold by Wall Street to unsuspecting investors), which should have been a canary-in-the-coal-mine warning but was ignored, so the same mistakes were repeated with conventional homes in 2004-07.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2008 letter (2008_p0059, 2008_p0060); unit=qualitative statement. 2008_p0059 describes the 1997-2000 manufactured-housing practices; 2008_p0060 links them to the 2004-07 conventional-housing bust.

gold_claims.claim: Lenders and borrowers alike counted on house-price appreciation to make otherwise impossible loans work.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2008 letter (2008_p0061); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: Most foreclosures happen not because a house is worth less than its mortgage ('upside-down' loans) but because borrowers cannot make the monthly payments they agreed to.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2008 letter (2008_p0065); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: If home buyers across the country had behaved like Clayton's, with a meaningful down-payment and fixed payments set at a sensible share of income, America would not have had the crisis it did.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2010 letter (2010_p0097); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: Everyone took part, including government, lenders, borrowers, the media and rating agencies, driven by the almost universal belief that house values were certain to rise.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2011 letter (2011_p0097); unit=qualitative statement

cases.verification_note: 2008_p0059, 2008_p0060, 2008_p0061, 2008_p0065, 2010_p0097, 2011_p0097 supply the 5 claims (lenders who shouldn't have lent + canary; house-price appreciation; upside-down; meaningful down-payment; rating agencies).

cases.query: Why did Buffett worry about the U.S. trade deficit and the dollar in the late 1980s and again in the 2000s, and what did Berkshire do about it?

gold_claims.claim: In 1987 he warned that the huge trade deficit was piling up 'claim checks' such as U.S. bonds and bank deposits in foreign hands, with the government relying, like Blanche DuBois, on the kindness of strangers.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1987 letter (1987_p0101); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: He feared that a government owing so much in its own currency would be pushed to inflate it away, calling the weapon of inflation the economic equivalent of the 'H' bomb for a debtor government.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1987 letter (1987_p0102); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: In 2002 he entered the foreign currency market for the first time in his life, and enlarged the position in 2003 as he grew increasingly bearish on the dollar.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2003 letter (2003_p0119); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: By year-end 2004 Berkshire held about $21.4 billion of foreign-exchange contracts spread among 12 currencies, because trade policies would keep pressing on the dollar for years.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2004 letter (2004_p0116); unit=figure

gold_claims.claim: In 2005 Berkshire reduced its direct currency position and preferred to get non-dollar exposure by owning equities that earn much of their profits abroad, because rising U.S. rates made holding most foreign currencies a negative carry.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2005 letter (2005_p0105); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: In 2007 he explained that because Americans buy more foreign goods than the world buys from the U.S., the country ships about $2 billion of IOUs and assets abroad every day, which pressures the dollar.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2007 letter (2007_p0092); unit=figure

cases.verification_note: 1987_p0101, 1987_p0102, 2003_p0119, 2004_p0116, 2005_p0105, 2007_p0092 supply the 6 claims (claim checks; weapon of inflation; bearish on the dollar; $21.4 billion; foreign currencies + carry; $2 billion of IOUs).

cases.query: Did Buffett say anything about the oil crisis in the 80s, and did he explain how the oil embargo hit the U.S. economy?

gold_claims.claim: In 1994 he listed 'two oil shocks' among the events of the previous 30 years that no one could have foreseen, as a reason to ignore political and economic forecasts.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1994 letter (1994_p0004); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: Looking back in 2023, he recalled that in 1975 the U.S. was woefully dependent on foreign oil, producing only eight million barrels of oil-equivalent a day, and that the government created the Strategic Petroleum Reserve that year.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2023 letter (2023_p0031, 2023_p0032); unit=qualitative statement

gold_claims.claim: Shale economics ended that dependence after 2011, so that OPEC no longer has the upper hand.
required_terms: OPEC no longer has the upper hand
gold_claims.verification_note: 2023 letter (2023_p0032); unit=qualitative statement

optional_claims.claim: In 1979 he noted that Berkshire's 1964 book value bought about half an ounce of gold and still bought about the same 15 years later, and that the same was true of Middle Eastern oil: government can print money but cannot print gold or create oil.
required_terms: unable to print gold or create oil

cases.answer_note: A correct answer says the letters describe no 1980s oil crisis (the embargo was 1973, the second shock 1979) and must not invent one, then gives what the letters do say.
cases.expected_coverage_note: User example question. The letters never discuss the oil crisis or the oil embargo directly; they mention oil only in passing ('two oil shocks' in 1994, a 2023 look back at 1975 oil dependence; optionally the 1979 gold/oil comparison). A correct answer reports these passing remarks, says the letters give no analysis of the embargo's effect on the economy, and does not invent one.
cases.verification_note: 1994_p0004, 2023_p0031, 2023_p0032 supply the 3 gold claims (two oil shocks; woefully dependent on foreign oil; OPEC no longer has the upper hand). The 1979 gold/oil remark (1979_p0014, Middle Eastern oil) is an optional claim, so 1979_p0014 is kept in relevant_ids only. Other passing oil mentions: 1982_p0042 ('OPEC-style' cartelization), 2007_p0095 ('not the fault of OPEC'). Whole-corpus case-insensitive searches for oil crisis, oil embargo, energy crisis have zero matches; no 1980s letter discusses an oil crisis.

cases.query: In year 1999, does Buffet suggest any sector that have potential to grow substantially?

gold_claims.claim: He did not recommend technology: he shared the general view that tech companies' products and services would transform society, but Berkshire owned no tech stocks because he had no insight into which tech companies had a truly durable competitive advantage.
required_terms: transformed by their products and services
gold_claims.verification_note: 1999 letter (1999_p0090, 1999_p0091): why Berkshire owns no tech stocks.

gold_claims.claim: Predicting the long-term economics of companies in fast-changing industries is beyond Berkshire's circle of competence, so it sticks with what it understands instead of envying those who claim that skill.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1999 letter (1999_p0092): circle of competence and fast-changing industries.

gold_claims.claim: Instead of tipping a growth sector, he warned that equity investors were wildly optimistic about future returns and that the coming market adjustment was apt to be severe, especially in sectors where speculation had been concentrated.
required_terms: sectors in which speculation has been concentrated
gold_claims.verification_note: 1999 letter (1999_p0094, 1999_p0095): GDP-linked return math and warning about speculative sectors.

gold_claims.claim: The one field he flagged for possible large new commitments was the electric utility industry (through the MidAmerican deal), despite its regulatory constraints.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1999 letter (1999_p0063): possible further utility commitments.

gold_claims.claim: Even for the fine businesses Berkshire already owned, the stock prices were not attractive, so he felt better about the businesses than their stocks and did not add to those holdings.
required_terms: much better about the businesses than their stocks
gold_claims.verification_note: 1999 letter (1999_p0093): prices of owned businesses not attractive.

cases.verification_note: User's own 1999 sector question (kept verbatim). Honest answer: no growth sector recommended; tech avoided (1999_p0090-p0092), market and speculative sectors judged overpriced (1999_p0093-p0095), only utilities flagged for possible large commitments (1999_p0063).

cases.query: Why did Buffett make a huge bet on railroads after the 2008 financial crisis, and what warning did he give about railroad earnings figures?

gold_claims.claim: He expected owning BNSF to raise Berkshire's normal earning power by nearly 40% pre-tax.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2010 letter (2010_p0010): BNSF effect on normal earning power.

gold_claims.claim: Railroads have major cost and environmental advantages over trucking: BNSF moved a ton of freight 500 miles on one gallon of diesel, about three times more fuel-efficient than trucks.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2010 letter (2010_p0012): rail versus trucking.

gold_claims.claim: U.S. freight movement will grow, the railroad will need massive investment, and Berkshire can supply the funds however slow the economy.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2010 letter (2010_p0013): growth and capital needs of BNSF.

gold_claims.claim: He called the BNSF purchase, agreed amid the gloom of the Great Recession, an all-in wager on the economic future of the United States.
required_terms: all-in wager on the economic future of the United States
gold_claims.verification_note: 2013 letter (2013_p0030): BNSF as a bet on America.

gold_claims.claim: His caveat: a railroad's depreciation charge falls far short of the capital spending needed just to keep it running, so its GAAP earnings are higher than true economic earnings.
required_terms: falls far short of the capital outlays
gold_claims.verification_note: 2015 letter (2015_p0090): inadequate railroad depreciation and EBITDA warning.

cases.verification_note: 2010_p0010, 2010_p0012, 2010_p0013, 2013_p0030, 2015_p0090 supply the 5 claims (nearly 40% pre-tax; fuel efficiency; invest massively; all-in wager; depreciation shortfall).

cases.query: What does Buffett think of the economics of the property-casualty insurance industry, and why does the industry as a whole earn poor returns?

gold_claims.claim: Insurance is a textbook case of an industry facing the deadly combination of excess capacity and a commodity product.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1982 letter (1982_p0048): insurance as excess capacity plus commodity product.

gold_claims.claim: The industry has dismal economic characteristics (hundreds of competitors, ease of entry, an undifferentiated product), so only very low-cost operators or protected niches earn high profits.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1987 letter (1987_p0045): poor long-term outlook for insurers.

gold_claims.claim: Like other commodity businesses it prospers only under shortage conditions, and insurance managers rushed to add capacity when shortages appeared in 1985-87.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1987 letter (1987_p0046): shortages and capacity expansion.

gold_claims.claim: Customers don't care which insurer they buy from, so price competition is usually fierce, like airline seats.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2004 letter (2004_p0035): why insurers earn poor returns.

gold_claims.claim: Industry premiums were inadequate to cover claims plus expenses in 37 of the 45 years ending in 2011, so cost-free float is not to be expected for the P/C industry as a whole.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2012 letter (2012_p0040): industry underwriting record.

gold_claims.claim: Every insurer's wish for underwriting profit creates intense competition, so despite its float income the industry will keep earning subnormal returns on tangible net worth compared with other American businesses.
required_terms: subnormal returns on tangible net worth
gold_claims.verification_note: 2016 letter (2016_p0043, 2016_p0044): competitive dynamics and the industry's returns.

cases.verification_note: 1982_p0048, 1987_p0045, 1987_p0046, 2004_p0035, 2012_p0040, 2016_p0043/p0044 supply the 6 claims (textbook case; dismal economic characteristics; shortage conditions; commodity-like product; 37 of the 45 years; subnormal returns). The former 2012+2016 claim is split per letter.

cases.query: How has Buffett's opinion of long-term bonds as an investment changed from the 1980s to 2020?

gold_claims.claim: In 1984 he disliked most long-term bonds because they are only as sound as a dollar and he expected substantial inflation ahead.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1984 letter (1984_p0107): dislike of long-term bonds.

gold_claims.claim: He kept his aversion to long-term bonds, the exception being the WPPSS bonds bought when they yielded around 17% after taxes, which worked out about as expected.
gold_claims.verification_note: 1988 letter (1988_p0074, 1988_p0075): aversion to bonds and the WPPSS exception.

gold_claims.claim: In late 2008 he said clinging to cash equivalents or long-term government bonds at present yields was almost certainly a terrible policy if continued for long, since their purchasing power would erode.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2008 letter (2008_p0094): long-term government bonds at crisis-era yields.

gold_claims.claim: In 2011 he said current rates did not compensate for purchasing-power risk, so bonds should come with a warning label and were priced to deliver return-free risk.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2011 letter (2011_p0114, 2011_p0116): currency-based investments.

gold_claims.claim: In 2017 he argued that purportedly risk-free long-term bonds in 2012 had been a far riskier investment than a long-term investment in common stocks, because even low inflation erodes their purchasing power.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2017 letter (2017_p0073): risk redefined as loss of purchasing power.

gold_claims.claim: In 2020 he said bonds are not the place to be: the 10-year Treasury yield of 0.93% had fallen 94% from 1981, and fixed-income investors face a bleak future.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2020 letter (2020_p0029): low bond yields.

cases.verification_note: 1984_p0107, 1988_p0074/p0075, 2008_p0094, 2011_p0114/p0116, 2017_p0073, 2020_p0029 supply the 6 claims (sound as a dollar; WPPSS 17%; terrible policy; warning label; far riskier investment; 0.93%).

cases.query: Why does Berkshire keep such a large cash pile, and does Buffett actually prefer cash to stocks?

gold_claims.claim: Cash is to a business what oxygen is to a person, unnoticed until it is missing; in the 2008 panic Berkshire could supply $15.6 billion to American businesses in three weeks.
required_terms: as oxygen is to an individual
gold_claims.verification_note: 2014 letter (2014_p0199): cash as oxygen.

gold_claims.claim: Berkshire customarily keeps at least $20 billion (usually far more, held in U.S. Treasury bills) so it can both withstand unprecedented insurance losses and quickly seize acquisition or investment opportunities, even during financial turmoil.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2010 letter (2010_p0139): the two-part reason; 2014 letter (2014_p0200) supports the $20 billion floor in Treasury bills.

gold_claims.claim: In 2021 he and Munger pledged that Berkshire will always hold more than $30 billion of cash and equivalents so it is financially impregnable and never dependent on the kindness of strangers.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2021 letter (2021_p0040): the raised cash floor.

gold_claims.claim: He accepts that this cash earns a pittance because it lets him sleep well.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2009 letter (2009_p0022): price of financial strength.

gold_claims.claim: He warns that crowds say 'cash is king' at the wrong time, as in late 2008 when cash should have been deployed rather than held.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2011 letter (2011_p0123): cash at peaks of fear.

gold_claims.claim: In 2024 he stressed that despite the large cash position the great majority of shareholders' money stays in equities, and Berkshire will never prefer cash-equivalents over owning good businesses.
required_terms: great majority of your money remains in equities
never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets
gold_claims.verification_note: 2024 letter (2024_p0025, 2024_p0026): equities over cash.

cases.verification_note: 2014_p0199, 2010_p0139 (+2014_p0200), 2021_p0040, 2009_p0022, 2011_p0123, 2024_p0025/p0026 supply the 6 claims (oxygen; at least $20 billion + insurance losses; $30 billion; sleep well; cash is king; majority in equities).

cases.query: How has Berkshire's own share-repurchase policy changed from its 2011 buyback authorization to the 2020s?

gold_claims.claim: In 2011 Berkshire authorized buybacks at up to 110% of book value; he favours repurchases only when a company has ample funds and its stock sells at a material discount to intrinsic value, conservatively calculated.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2011 letter (2011_p0031, 2011_p0032): Berkshire's repurchase authorization and the two conditions.

gold_claims.claim: The 110% limit proved unrealistic, so in December 2012 Berkshire raised it to 120% of book value when a large block became available at about 116% of book.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2012 letter (2012_p0114, 2012_p0115): limit raised to 120%.

gold_claims.claim: By 2018 he framed repurchases by intrinsic value rather than a book-value limit: Berkshire would likely be a significant repurchaser at prices above book value but below its estimate of intrinsic value, and repurchases must be price-sensitive.
required_terms: below our estimate of intrinsic value
gold_claims.verification_note: 2018 letter (2018_p0017, 2018_p0037, 2018_p0038): the switch to the intrinsic-value standard.

gold_claims.claim: In 2020-2021 Berkshire repurchased 9% of its shares for $51.7 billion, while he insisted overpaying for its own shares would be value-destroying.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2021 letter (2021_p0045): two years of large repurchases.

gold_claims.claim: In 2022 Berkshire repurchased 1.2% of its shares, and he defended value-accretive repurchases: people who say all repurchases harm shareholders or the country are economic illiterates or silver-tongued demagogues.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2022 letter (2022_p0027-p0029): 2022 repurchases and defence of buybacks.

cases.verification_note: Re-focused on Berkshire's own repurchase policy (fixlist DECISION). 2011_p0031/p0032, 2012_p0114/p0115, 2018_p0017/p0037/p0038, 2021_p0045, 2022_p0027-p0029 supply the 5 claims (110% of book; 120%; below our estimate of intrinsic value; $51.7 billion; 1.2% + economic illiterate). The general principles (1984_p0018, 1999_p0100/p0101) stay gold in fin_g5_06 and are not gold here.

cases.query: Why doesn't Berkshire pay a dividend, and how does Buffett think a company should choose between paying dividends and retaining earnings?

gold_claims.claim: Earnings should be retained only when each dollar retained is likely to create at least one dollar of market value for owners.
required_terms: at least one dollar of market value
gold_claims.verification_note: 1984 letter (1984_p0115): the one valid reason for retention.

gold_claims.claim: Because Berkshire earned well above market rates on retained earnings, any distribution would have been contrary to shareholders' financial interest.
required_terms: contrary to the financial interest of shareholders
gold_claims.verification_note: 1984 letter (1984_p0128): dividend principles applied to Berkshire.

gold_claims.claim: His 2012 example showed that a sell-off approach (owners selling a few shares each year) leaves them with about 4% more value and more cash than a dividend policy.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2012 letter (2012_p0120): sell-off versus dividend math.

gold_claims.claim: Dividends force one cash-out policy on every shareholder and are taxed in full, while a sell-off is taxed only on the gain portion.
required_terms: tax on only the gain portion
gold_claims.verification_note: 2012 letter (2012_p0122, 2012_p0124): two further arguments against dividends.

cases.verification_note: Superlative weighed over the whole corpus: P/C insurance is praised as core business / engine in 20 letters 1995-2024 plus 1990 ('greatest potential'); 9 gold passages from 8 letters supply the 4 claims (core and engine; float as fountain of funds; praise across decades; caveat on industry economics).

cases.query: How did Buffett's opinion of the airline industry change over the years?

gold_claims.claim: Around 1989 he said he had no ability to forecast the economics of the airline industry ('agnostics, not atheists'), so Berkshire had to structure any investment in it differently from investments in businesses with splendid economics.

In the early 1990s he said industry economics deteriorated at an alarming pace because of kamikaze pricing; in a commodity business you cannot be much smarter than your dumbest competitor, and the industry has lost money in aggregate since Kitty Hawk.
gold_claims.verification_note: Required terms in the 1990 letter (1990_p0102); the 1991 letter (1991_p0090, 'net loss since its birth after Kitty Hawk') supports.

gold_claims.claim: By 1994 he blamed deregulation: in an unregulated commodity business high-cost carriers must lower their costs to competitive levels or face extinction, a rule he admitted he had missed when Berkshire put capital into USAir.
In 2007 he used airlines as the example of the worst sort of business (fast growth, heavy capital, little profit): investors poured money into a bottomless pit, and he bought USAir 'to my shame'.
By 2016 Berkshire had made large investments in America's four major carriers, and he wrote of a tolerance 'bordering on enthusiasm' for airlines.
gold_claims.verification_note: 2016 letter (2016_p0152); holdings tables 2016-2019 (Delta, Southwest, United) are in relevant_ids.

cases.verification_note: All airline passages in the corpus were read (22 letters mention airlines; many are annual-meeting travel notes). Gold passages from 6 letters (1989-2016) supply the 5 claims of the industry arc (agnostic; kamikaze pricing; deregulation; worst business and the USAir regret; 2016 investments in four carriers). The USAir-specific passages 1994_p0085 and 1996_p0098 and the 1992 'competitive tontine' passage 1992_p0082 stay in relevant_ids only, because fin_g2_02 now covers the USAir investment.

cases.query: How has Buffett's view of newspapers as a business changed across his letters?

gold_claims.claim: In the 1980s he called the economics of a dominant newspaper among the very best in the business world: once dominant, even a poor paper prospers.
required_terms: among the very best in the business world
Good or bad, it will prosper

gold_claims.claim: From 1990-1991 he warned that media businesses would prove considerably less marvelous than expected and that newspapers had begun to behave more like ordinary businesses than franchises.
gold_claims.verification_note: Required term in the 1991 letter (1991_p0022); the 1990 letter (1990_p0038, 'considerably less marvelous') supports.

gold_claims.claim: In 1995 he said the industry had lost still another notch and that newspapers' competitive strength would gradually erode, though it would remain a fine business for years.
By 2006 fundamentals were definitely eroding: papers were losing the battle for eyeballs, and had cable, satellite and the internet come first, newspapers probably would never have existed.

Even so, in 2011-2012 Berkshire bought 28 daily newspapers for $344 million while he still predicted industry decline, because local papers remain indispensable; he would buy more only at a very low multiple of current earnings.
required_terms: very low multiple of current earnings
gold_claims.verification_note: 2012 letter (2012_p0091, 2012_p0105); 2015_p0139 (circulation will keep falling) is in relevant_ids.

gold_claims.claim: He and Munger believe papers that deliver comprehensive and reliable information to tightly-bound communities and have a sensible Internet strategy will remain viable for a long time.

cases.verification_note: All newspaper passages were read (27 letters mention newspapers; most are Buffalo News operating detail). Gold passages from 6 letters 1984-2012 supply the 6 claims (dominant paper economics; less marvelous and businesses more than franchises; another notch; eroding fundamentals; 2012 purchase at low multiples; papers serving tightly-bound communities remain viable).

cases.query: What does Buffett keep repeating about when share buybacks make sense?

gold_claims.claim: Buying back shares when a fine business sells far below intrinsic value is one of the most certain and profitable uses of capital; such buybacks often get $2 of present value for $1.
gold_claims.verification_note: Required term in the 1984 letter (1984_p0018); the 1980 letter (1980_p0011, 'far less than intrinsic value') supports.

gold_claims.claim: Two conditions must hold: the company has funds beyond the needs of the business, and its stock sells below intrinsic value, conservatively calculated.
gold_claims.verification_note: Required terms in the 2011 letter (2011_p0032); the 1999 letter (1999_p0097, 'beyond the near-term needs of the business') and the 2019 letter (2019_p0077, 'selling for less than it is worth', 'ample cash') support.

gold_claims.claim: Price is everything: what is smart at one price is dumb at another, and buying above intrinsic value (dollar bills for $1.10) destroys value for continuing shareholders.
required_terms: smart at one price is dumb at another
gold_claims.verification_note: Required term in the 2011 letter (2011_p0033); the 1999 letter (1999_p0100, 'dollar bills for $1.10') and the 2012 letter (2012_p0116, 'price is all-important') support.

gold_claims.claim: He criticizes managements that repurchase to support the price or 'show confidence', and American CEOs' embarrassing record of buying back more when prices have risen than when they have fallen.
gold_claims.verification_note: Required term in the 1999 letter (1999_p0101); the 2020 letter (2020_p0034, 'embarrassing record') supports.

gold_claims.claim: He defends value-accretive buybacks against blanket critics who call them un-American or harmful: such critics are economic illiterates or silver-tongued demagogues.
gold_claims.verification_note: Required term in the 2016 letter (2016_p0039); the 2022 letter (2022_p0029, 'economic illiterate') supports.

cases.verification_note: Repurchase passages in all 35 letters that mention them were scanned. Gold passages from 9 letters 1980-2022 supply the 5 claims (below-value buybacks create value; two conditions; price is all-important; criticism of CEOs; defense against critics).

cases.query: What kind of business does Buffett consistently describe as the best kind to own?

gold_claims.claim: The best businesses earn high returns on capital and need little incremental investment to grow; the rare ideal could reinvest large sums at very high rates of return.
gold_claims.verification_note: Required term in the 2009 letter (2009_p0051); the 1992 letter (1992_p0072, 'very high rates of return') supports.

gold_claims.claim: He prefers an economic franchise: a product that is needed, has no close substitute and is not price-regulated, so it can price aggressively and earn high returns.
A truly great business needs an enduring moat, such as being the low-cost producer or having a powerful worldwide brand like Coca-Cola or Gillette.
gold_claims.verification_note: Required term in both the 1993 letter (1993_p0074, 'protective moat') and the 2007 letter (2007_p0028, 'enduring moat', 'powerful world-wide brand').

gold_claims.claim: See's Candies is his model: it earned about 60% pre-tax on invested capital, had durable pricing power, and grew earnings with virtually no major capital requirements.
gold_claims.verification_note: Required terms in the 2007 letter (2007_p0034, '60% pre-tax on invested capital'); 2007_p0038 ('virtually no major capital requirements') and the 2014 letter (2014_p0155, 'significant pricing power') support.

gold_claims.claim: It is better to buy a wonderful business at a fair price than a fair business at a wonderful price, because time is the friend of the wonderful business and the enemy of the mediocre.
gold_claims.verification_note: Required terms in the 2014 letter (2014_p0153, 'wonderful businesses at fair prices'); the 1989 letter (1989_p0127, 'Time is the friend of the wonderful business') and the 1979 letter (1979_p0025, 'good business purchased at a fair price') support.

cases.verification_note: Best/great/wonderful business, moat and franchise passages were scanned across all letters. Gold passages from 8 letters 1979-2014 supply the 5 claims (high returns with little capital; economic franchise; enduring moat; See's model; wonderful business at a fair price).
